lead: At a regular singular point x0, a plain Taylor series can fail because the coefficients of y′ and y blow up. The Frobenius method multiplies the series by (x − x0)^r. The exponent r is not assumed integer and is found first from the indicial equation. Then a recurrence gives the coefficients. This solves Bessel and Legendre equations near a singular boundary, including vibration of a circular membrane at its centre. Bessel's equation is solved this way in 3.5.
prereq: You need 3.1 for regular singular classification and 3.2 for shifting indices in series products.

sections.h3: From singular point to indicial equation

blocks.text: At a regular singular point x0, write the ODE as y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = 0. A singular point is regular when (x − x0)P(x) and (x − x0)²Q(x) are analytic at x0. For the rational coefficients in most B.Tech examples, this reduces to finite limits after removing the pole. Define p0 = lim<sub>x→x0</sub> (x − x0)P(x) and q0 = lim<sub>x→x0</sub> (x − x0)²Q(x). For x0 = 0 these are p0 = lim xP and q0 = lim x²Q.

A Taylor series can fail because P and Q are not analytic there. Frobenius inserts an unknown power: y = (x − x0)^r Σ a<sub>n</sub>(x − x0)^n = Σ a<sub>n</sub>(x − x0)<sup>n+r</sup>, with a<sub>0</sub> ≠ 0. The number r need not be an integer.

Multiply the ODE by (x − x0)² before substituting. Then the lowest power is (x − x0)^r, and its coefficient is a0[r(r − 1) + p0 r + q0]. In the original standard form the corresponding power is (x − x0)^(r−2). Setting the coefficient to zero gives the indicial equation. Its roots r<sub>1</sub>, r<sub>2</sub> are the indicial roots. They fix the form of the solution before any coefficient is computed. Putting r = 0 recovers the ordinary power-series case.

blocks.where: r is the unknown exponent; p<sub>0</sub> and q<sub>0</sub> are the limits defined above; F(r) = 0 is the indicial equation.

blocks.text: Let r<sub>1</sub> ≥ r<sub>2</sub> be real roots of the indicial equation.

items: r<sub>1</sub> − r<sub>2</sub> not an integer: two independent Frobenius series exist, one from each root.

r<sub>1</sub> − r<sub>2</sub> a positive integer: r<sub>1</sub> always gives a Frobenius series. r<sub>2</sub> may give one, or the recurrence may break. Then y<sub>2</sub> = C y<sub>1</sub> ln(x − x<sub>0</sub>) + (x − x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>r<sub>2</sub></sup> Σ b<sub>n</sub>(x − x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>n</sup>.
r<sub>1</sub> = r<sub>2</sub>: one series comes from r<sub>1</sub>. The second generally contains a logarithm, with the same form as above.

blocks.text: For complex roots r = α ± iβ, solutions carry (x − x0)^α cos(β ln|x − x0|) and (x − x0)^α sin(β ln|x − x0|). These are real on either side of x0. Most exams ask only for the larger real root; state the log form when roots are equal or differ by an integer. Some syllabi call this the Frobenius method at a regular singularity.

sections.h3: Building the series for the larger root

items: Confirm x0 is regular singular. Put the ODE in standard form.
Compute p0 and q0 from the limits.
Assume y = (x − x0)^r1 Σ a_n (x − x0)^n, with a0 ≠ 0.
After multiplying by (x − x0)², substitute and set the coefficient of (x − x0)^(n+r1) to zero; in standard form set the coefficient of (x − x0)^(n+r1−2) to zero. This gives a recurrence.
Set a0 = 1, compute a1, a2, ... and write y1.

blocks.text: The recurrence usually contains the bracket (n + r1)(n + r1 − 1) + p0(n + r1) + q0. For the larger root this bracket is nonzero for n ≥ 1, so division is safe. For the smaller root it can vanish, which is exactly where a logarithm or a free second series appears. The n = 0 equation is the indicial equation and puts no condition on a0.

figure.caption: The flowchart starts at the regular singular point x = 0, uses p0 = −1/2 and q0 = 1/2 to form 2r² − 3r + 1 = 0, and takes roots r = 1 and r = 1/2 before the recurrence. The recurrence shown applies to r1 = 1.

spec.title: Frobenius method
spec.aria: A flowchart starts at a regular singular point, computes p0 and q0, forms 2r squared minus 3r plus 1 equals 0, takes roots 1 and 1 half, then uses a recurrence for the series when r1 equals 1.

nodes.label: Assume y = x^r Σ a_n x^n

examples.question: Use the Frobenius method at x = 0 for 2x²y″ − xy′ + (1 + x)y = 0. Find the indicial roots and the series for the larger root through x⁴.
steps: Divide by 2x²: y″ − (1/(2x))y′ + (1 + x)/(2x²)y = 0. So P = −1/(2x) and Q = (1 + x)/(2x²).
Indicial equation: r(r − 1) − r/2 + 1/2 = 0. Multiply by 2: 2r² − 3r + 1 = 0 = (2r − 1)(r − 1). Roots r1 = 1 and r2 = 1/2.
Take r = 1. Assume y = Σ a_n x^(n+1). Then y′ = Σ (n+1)a_n x^n and y″ = Σ n(n+1)a_n x^(n−1).
Substitute: 2x²y″ = Σ 2n(n+1)a_n x^(n+1); −xy′ = Σ −(n+1)a_n x^(n+1); y = Σ a_n x^(n+1); xy = Σ a_n x^(n+2).
Coefficient of x^(n+1): [2n(n+1) − (n+1) + 1]a_n + a_(n−1) = 0. The bracket is 2n² + n = n(2n+1). So n(2n+1)a_n + a_(n−1) = 0.
Recurrence: a_n = −a_(n−1)/[n(2n+1)] for n ≥ 1. Set a0 = 1.
Since 1 − 1/2 = 1/2 is not an integer, a second independent Frobenius series comes from r = 1/2.
examples.answer: The indicial roots are r = 1 and r = 1/2; for r = 1, y1 = x(1 − x/3 + x²/30 − x³/630 + x⁴/22680 − ...).
examples.check:
from math import sqrt
p0 = -1/2
q0 = 1/2
b = p0 - 1
disc = b*b - 4*q0
r1 = (-b + sqrt(disc))/2
r2 = (-b - sqrt(disc))/2
print(f'{p0:.1f}')
print(f'{q0:.1f}')
print(f'{r1:.1f}')
print(f'{r2:.1f}')
a = 1.0
for n in range(1,5):
    a = -a/(n*(2*n+1))
    print(f'{a:.6f}')

traps: Using r where n + r belongs in the recurrence. The bracket must carry n + r, not r alone.
Dividing by a0 or setting a0 = 0. The leading coefficient a0 is free and must stay nonzero.
Assuming the smaller root always gives an independent ordinary Frobenius series. When roots differ by an integer, the second solution may need a logarithm.
Taking p0 = lim P and q0 = lim Q. The correct limits are p0 = lim (x − x0)P and q0 = lim (x − x0)²Q.
Forgetting to shift the index in the x·y product, so the recurrence is off by one.

quiz.q: Write the indicial equation at a regular singular point x0.
quiz.a: F(r) = r(r − 1) + p0 r + q0 = 0, where p<sub>0</sub> = lim<sub>x→x0</sub> (x − x<sub>0</sub>)P(x) and q<sub>0</sub> = lim<sub>x→x0</sub> (x − x<sub>0</sub>)²Q(x).

quiz.q: Why must a0 ≠ 0 in the Frobenius assumption y = (x − x0)^r Σ a_n (x − x0)^n?
quiz.a: If a0 = 0, the lowest power is no longer (x − x0)^r, so the indicial equation would change. Keeping a0 ≠ 0 fixes r as the true leading exponent.

quiz.q: For x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − 1/4)y = 0 at x = 0, find p0, q0 and the indicial roots.
quiz.a: P = 1/x and Q = 1 − 1/(4x²). Thus p0 = 1 and q0 = −1/4. The indicial equation is r(r − 1) + r − 1/4 = r² − 1/4 = 0, so r = 1/2 and r = −1/2.

quiz.q: Why does Frobenius multiply by x^r instead of using a plain power series?
quiz.a: Near a regular singular point, P or Q blows up, so a Taylor series is not guaranteed. The factor x^r allows a fractional or negative leading power and restores a valid series form.

quiz.q: The indicial roots are 3 and 1. What can you say about the two solutions?
quiz.a: The larger root r = 3 always gives a Frobenius series. The smaller root r = 1 may give a Frobenius series, or the recurrence may break and the second solution may contain a logarithm. Check the recurrence at the smaller root.

quiz.q: If p0 = 0 and q0 = 0, solve the indicial equation.
For the larger root r1, why is division by (n + r1)(n + r1 − 1) + p0(n + r1) + q0 safe for n ≥ 1?
quiz.a: At r = r1 this bracket equals n(n + r1 − r2). For n ≥ 1 it is nonzero, so the recurrence can be divided through without a zero denominator.

beyond: Not for the exam. Frobenius expansions are a first step in analysing singularities of special functions; numerical libraries use them near endpoints where Taylor series are unstable. In perturbation theory, the exponent r reveals boundary-layer behaviour. Search for “Frobenius method”, “indicial equation”, “regular singular point” and “logarithmic solution”.
